title: How much is it?
goal: Say and understand numbers, ask about prices, and get to grips with the number rule that is both the most confusing and the most used.
bekal: count from one to a hundred
ask about price and quantity with *bikam* and *kam*
say how many things there are in the correct form

dialogs.title: حِوَار — فِي مَحَلِّ الْقِرْطَاسِيَّةِ
dialogs.intro: Budi is buying school supplies at a stationery shop near the campus.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Peace be upon you. Do you have notebooks?

lines.speaker: اَلْبَائِع:
lines.id: And upon you be peace. Yes, here you are.
lines.literal: and upon you(pl) peace. yes, please.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.baca: uriidu thalaathata dafaatira wa khamsata aqlaam.
lines.id: I'd like three notebooks and five pens.
lines.literal: I-want three notebooks and five pens.

lines.speaker: اَلْبَائِع:
lines.id: The pens are five pounds each.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: So how much is the total?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: هٰذَا غَالٍ قَلِيلًا. هَلْ عِنْدَكُمْ أَرْخَصُ؟
lines.id: That's a bit expensive. Do you have anything cheaper?

lines.speaker: اَلْبَائِع:
lines.id: Yes, this one is just three pounds.
lines.literal: yes, this for three pounds only.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: OK. Here you are, fifty pounds.

lines.speaker: اَلْبَائِع:
lines.id: And here's your change. Thank you, goodbye!
lines.literal: and this the-remainder. thanks, with the-safety!

notes: **بِكَمْ literally "for how much".** The بِ here marks the price — like English "for". The answer uses بِ too: بِعَشَرَةِ جُنَيْهَاتٍ. Answering with the bare number (just عَشَرَة) is also common in quick conversation.

**كَمِ الْمَجْمُوعُ — a kasra out of nowhere.** كَمْ originally ends in a sukun, but when it meets the اَلْ of the next word, two vowelless letters collide and the sukun becomes a kasra: *kamil-majmuu'*. You already saw the same thing in مِنَ الْمَغْرِبِ in unit 2.

**The numbers 3–10 take the opposite gender.** ثَلَاثَةَ دَفَاتِرَ — the number is in the feminine form (ثَلَاثَة) even though دَفْتَر is masculine. This is not a typo but a rule, and it confuses learners more than any other. See the grammar box.

**From 11 up, the noun is SINGULAR with tanween fatha.** خَمْسُونَ جُنَيْهًا — "fifty pounds", with جُنَيْه in the singular, not جُنَيْهَات. That's the exact opposite of 3–10, which take the plural. English never makes you think about this at all.

**تَفَضَّلْ is used far more often than you'd expect.** It means "please / go ahead / here you are" in every situation: inviting someone in, handing something over, offering a seat, inviting someone to speak. To a woman: تَفَضَّلِي. To several people: تَفَضَّلُوا.

**غَالٍ — a word whose final ي drops.** The base form is غَالِي, but the ي disappears when the word is indefinite, leaving a tanween kasra: غَالٍ. Similar words: مُحَامٍ (lawyer), نَادٍ (club). You only need to recognize these for now, not form them yourself.

**أَرْخَص — the "-er" form.** The pattern أَفْعَل expresses comparison: رَخِيص (cheap) → أَرْخَص (cheaper); كَبِير (big) → أَكْبَر; جَيِّد (good) → أَجْوَد or أَحْسَن. This form doesn't change for gender — one form for all.
**طَيِّب is the Arabic "OK".** Literally "good", but in conversation it works exactly like "OK" or "all right": it signals agreement or a change of topic. In Egyptian dialect it's shortened to طَبْ.
**اَلْبَاقِي — the change.** Literally "what remains". If you don't want your change: اِحْتَفِظْ بِالْبَاقِي ("keep the change").

grammars.title: Numbers 1 to 10 — and their reverse rule
body: The numbers 1 and 2 behave like ordinary adjectives and agree with their noun. The numbers 3 to 10 do the opposite, and that is the part that needs attention.
after: **The rule: numbers 3–10 take the form OPPOSITE to their noun.** A masculine noun (كِتَاب) gets a number in the feminine form (ثَلَاثَة); a feminine noun (طَاوِلَة) gets a number without ة (ثَلَاث). There's no satisfying explanation — it simply is so, and you'll learn it far faster through examples than through the rule.
The noun changes too: after 3–10 it becomes **plural** with a kasra — ثَلَاثَةُ كُتُبٍ, not ثَلَاثَةُ كِتَابٍ.
The good news: in everyday speech across the Arab world, this rule is often relaxed. Your mistakes won't stop anyone from understanding you — but getting it right makes your Arabic sound educated.

grammars.title: Numbers from 11 up
after: **From 11 on, the noun is always SINGULAR with tanween fatha** (ـًا). So عِشْرُونَ جُنَيْهًا ("twenty pounds"), not جُنَيْهَات. Strange to an English speaker, but consistent.

In short there are only three cases: **1–2** ordinary noun · **3–10** plural with kasra · **11 and up** singular with fatha. If you only have time to memorize one thing from this page, make it those three lines.

blocks.text: The digits used in the West (1, 2, 3) do come from the Arab world — Europeans call them "Arabic numerals". But the eastern Arab world actually uses a different set, which comes from India. You'll see both in the street.

Notice that numbers are **still written left to right** even though the script runs right to left: ١٩٩٥ is read one thousand nine hundred ninety-five, not the other way round. This saves you from misreading a lot of phone numbers and prices.

blocks.title: Haggling: what to know before you try
items: In a traditional market (سُوق) haggling is normal and even expected. In modern shops, supermarkets and pharmacies, prices are fixed and haggling will feel awkward.

A polite phrase that works: هَلْ يُمْكِنُ تَخْفِيضٌ قَلِيلًا؟ ("could you take a little off?"). What doesn't work: offering half the price straight away. A fair offer is usually about two-thirds of the price quoted.
A closing line if you decide not to buy: شُكْرًا، سَأُفَكِّرُ (*shukran, sa'ufakkir* — "thanks, I'll think about it"). It's polite and commits you to nothing.

exercises.prompt: Write the number in Arabic words.
Read these prices out in words. Write your answers.
Build a short conversation in a shop: you want to buy two dictionaries and five pens, you ask for the total, and you find it too expensive.
items: Ask the price of the dictionary

answers: سَبْعَةُ كُتُبٍ — ثَلَاثُ طَاوِلَاتٍ — عَشَرَةُ أَقْلَامٍ — خَمْسُ سَاعَاتٍ — عِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا — خَمْسَةٌ وَأَرْبَعُونَ جُنَيْهًا
بِكَمْ هٰذَا الْكِتَابُ؟ — بِعِشْرِينَ جُنَيْهًا. — هٰذَا غَالٍ جِدًّا. — هَلْ عِنْدَكُمْ أَرْخَصُ؟ — أُرِيدُ ثَلَاثَةَ دَفَاتِرَ. — كَمِ الْمَجْمُوعُ؟
خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ جُنَيْهًا — ثَلَاثُونَ رِيَالًا — سَبْعَةُ دُولَارَاتٍ — مِائَةُ دِرْهَمٍ — اِثْنَانِ وَسِتُّونَ جُنَيْهًا

Example: اَلسَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ. — بِكَمْ هٰذَا الْقَامُوسُ؟ — أُرِيدُ قَامُوسَيْنِ وَخَمْسَةَ أَقْلَامٍ. — كَمِ الْمَجْمُوعُ؟ — هٰذَا غَالٍ قَلِيلًا، هَلْ عِنْدَكُمْ أَرْخَصُ؟ — شُكْرًا، مَعَ السَّلَامَةِ.
wave: Today, silently count whatever you see: three chairs, five windows, twenty stairs. In Arabic.
